name: BrowserOS neo
description: A Chromium-based browser plus local MCP server that lets external agents (Claude Code, Codex, Cursor and others) drive a logged-in browser.
scored_configuration: BrowserOS neo as installed from the README: default onboarding (Chrome import with default items), first-run auto-connect of detected agents, local MCP endpoint on loopback, remote MCP access off, telemetry on.
headline: BrowserOS neo hands connected agents your logged-in browser: default onboarding imports your Chrome logins, and every tool, including a scripting tool with raw DevTools Protocol access, works on any site and any tab with no approval step in the server. A hostile page that hijacks the agent can read and act in your accounts and send data anywhere. Agents can also save skills that are linked into your coding agents' skill folders and reused later, and the local cockpit API is not locked down by default. Scripts run in a bounded QuickJS engine and every action is recorded for replay, but keep neo away from accounts you can't afford to have misused.

criteria.name: Identity & least privilege
criteria.question: Does the agent act with an identity scoped to its job, with authority checked per request rather than inherited?
criteria.summary: BrowserOS neo is a separate browser, but its default onboarding imports the user's Chrome logins, history and other data, and agents then act with every signed-in session in that profile. The server has no identity of its own and no per-request authorization: tab ownership is shown to the agent as a label but the code deliberately never refuses an action on the user's or another agent's tab. The scripting tool also exposes the raw Chrome DevTools Protocol, which reaches the whole browser. The local cockpit API that manages connections, skills and sessions is not locked down by its default access configuration. A hijacked or misbehaving agent therefore holds the user's full web identity.

S.finding: A dedicated browser profile separates neo from the everyday browser, but it is populated with the user's imported logins and every tab and site is reachable, including through raw CDP.
S.gap: No per-capability or per-site scoping of the authority the agent receives.

C.finding: No authorization check sits on any tool path: ownership of tabs is only a label, and the instruction to act on one's own tabs is prompt text.
C.gap: No code-level authorization layer on tool dispatch.

evidence.contains: Ownership is a label, not a permission

D.finding: Default onboarding selects every import item except search engines and extensions, so the agent profile starts with the user's logins.
D.gap: Least-privilege default (empty profile, or per-site grants) is not the default.

B.finding: Authority covers every account the user is signed into in the browser, across services.
B.gap: Authority is not limited to one system or to reads.

criteria.name: Approval gates
criteria.question: Do consequential actions require a human's informed approval by default, with no path around the gate?
criteria.summary: As a tool server, neo leaves approval to the connected agent; its contribution is risk signalling. Read tools carry read-only hints, but the click, navigate, download and upload tools carry no annotations, the save-skill tool is marked non-destructive, and the main `run` tool mixes reads and writes in arbitrary scripts that the description tells agents to prefer for every task. There is no preview, no read-only mode and no server-enforced confirmation. A `request_human_help` tool lets the agent hand a tab to a person, but the agent decides when to use it. Actions in logged-in accounts (posting, sending, buying) are not reversible.

S.finding: Annotations exist (read-only on read tools) but are missing on mutating tools and inaccurate for save_skill, and the primary run tool mixes reads and writes.
S.gap: No separate read and write tools with accurate hints on every tool.

C.finding: Every request can go through the generic run tool, which a host approval sees as one opaque script.
C.gap: Mutating capability is not split into narrowly annotated tools.

D.finding: Hints are compiled in and always present; there is no read-only mode or server-side confirmation to switch on.
D.gap: No server-enforced read-only mode or confirmation step.

B.finding: A wrongly approved action can post, send, purchase or delete in any signed-in account, with no undo.
B.gap: No checkpoint, preview or dry-run for external actions.

criteria.name: Tool & action scoping
criteria.question: Is each tool the narrowest thing that does its job, with arguments validated in code against allowlists and bounds?
criteria.summary: Every tool has a typed argument schema that rejects unknown fields, but the arguments themselves are mostly passed through. `run` accepts arbitrary JavaScript against an SDK that includes raw DevTools Protocol access, `evaluate` runs arbitrary JavaScript in pages, navigation checks only a small scheme denylist, and `upload` attaches any local file path to a page's file input. All seventeen browser tools are enabled by default with no tool groups. A misused tool can act on any site the browser is signed into and send local files out.

S.finding: Validation is typed schemas plus a small URL-scheme denylist; the most powerful tools take arbitrary scripts and file paths.
S.gap: No allowlist validation (host allowlists, path containment) on URLs, scripts or upload paths.

evidence.contains: files must exist on the server filesystem

C.finding: Few arguments are validated beyond their type.
C.gap: Most built-in tools do not validate their arguments.

B.gap: Tools are not scoped to a site, workspace or quantity bound.

criteria.name: Code-execution isolation
criteria.question: When model-influenced code runs, does a boundary the model cannot redefine contain it on every path?
criteria.summary: Model-written code runs in two places. `run` scripts execute in a fresh QuickJS engine inside the server process, with no filesystem, network or process access of their own, a 64 MB memory limit, a stack limit and a 30-second interrupt; `evaluate` and `page.evaluate` run JavaScript inside Chrome's page renderer. The QuickJS engine is written in C, so an engine bug would land in the server process, and the injected SDK includes raw DevTools Protocol access with browser-wide control. The server process runs as the user, writes to connected agents' config and skill directories, and drives the signed-in browser.

S.finding: A capability-only QuickJS runtime per call (no ambient authority, memory and stack limits) plus the Chrome renderer for page scripts; the engine is not memory-safe, so it falls short of the capability-runtime anchor.
S.gap: Runtime is not written in a memory-safe language, and there is no OS-level isolation of the server.

evidence.contains: There is no fetch, require, process

C.finding: All model-reachable code paths run in QuickJS or the page renderer, but the injected raw CDP method gives scripts browser-level control outside the narrow SDK.
C.gap: The runtime's injected surface is not limited to bounded capabilities.

D.finding: The runtime is the only execution path, configured in compiled code that the model cannot change.
D.gap: Sandbox policy is fixed in code but the escape hatch is part of the default SDK.

B.finding: An engine escape lands in the server process running as the user, and the injected functions already reach the whole signed-in browser.
B.gap: Execution is not separated from the user's account and browser authority.

criteria.name: Untrusted input blast radius
criteria.question: When the agent reads untrusted content, what limits how far that content can steer it?
criteria.summary: Page text returned by the read, grep, snapshot, diff and evaluate tools is wrapped in per-call nonce markers with the page origin and a notice to treat it as data. Values returned from `run` scripts, the primary tool, are not wrapped. Nothing in the server limits what an agent can do after reading a hostile page: the same session can read private data in signed-in accounts, act in them, and send data anywhere. There is no read-only or no-egress mode.

cap.reason: Worst case (B L0): a hijacked agent can leak data and take irreversible actions unattended.

S.finding: Page-derived text carries provenance (origin) and an untrusted marker in structured results.
S.gap: No mode that drops a Rule-of-Two leg (read-only or no-egress).

C.finding: Granular read tools are wrapped, but run script results, which agents are told to prefer, are returned unmarked.
C.gap: Not every source of page content is marked.

D.finding: The wrapper is applied in code and cannot be turned off.
D.gap: Coverage gaps keep this from being a configuration-proof control.

B.finding: A hijacked agent can read private data in any signed-in account, exfiltrate it through navigation or uploads, and take irreversible actions, with no human involved.
B.gap: No structural block on egress or state change after untrusted content is read.

criteria.name: Memory, context & configuration integrity
criteria.question: Can anything the agent reads persist into future behaviour through memory, retrieval, or auto-loaded files, and is that path controlled?
criteria.summary: Agents can persist instructions and code. The `save_skill` tool writes a skill file and links it into every connected agent's user skills directory (for example ~/.claude/skills), where those agents load it in later sessions. `run` scripts can save JavaScript helpers per website, and successful runs are also distilled into helpers automatically; both are loaded into later runs on that host. Nothing validates or gates these writes, and they are shared across all agents and sessions. Skills are visible and deletable in the cockpit.

S.finding: The model can write skills and helper code that persist and are re-loaded as trusted instructions or code.
S.gap: No human approval or validation for persistent writes.

B.finding: A poisoned skill or helper persists across the user's sessions and agents and can drive tool use.
B.gap: Persistent content is not gated or reviewed before it affects behaviour.

criteria.name: Third-party extensions
criteria.question: Are plugins, MCP servers and downloaded tools verified or isolated before they run with the agent's access?
criteria.summary: The neo server loads no plugins and launches no MCP servers or packages at runtime; the only package command in the server is a stdio fallback for agents without HTTP transport, and every supported agent uses HTTP at system scope. Importing Chrome extensions is optional and off by default in onboarding. The project's own bundled components and updates are its own supply chain and out of scope here.

criteria.name: Secrets & sensitive-data protection
criteria.question: Are credentials and sensitive data kept out of logs, telemetry, subprocesses, and the model provider?
criteria.summary: The neo server holds no model or service API keys of its own; browser credentials stay in Chromium's store. Usage telemetry is on by default but built from allowlisted fingerprints so literals and page text are dropped, session recordings mask password inputs, and helper distillation drops typed values. The audit log stores tool arguments in plain form, and the model can read cookies and page data of any signed-in site through the browser tools, which are long-lived session credentials.

S.finding: Allowlist-based telemetry fingerprints, password masking in recordings and literal filtering in distillation.
S.gap: No redaction before audit storage or before model-bound results; no encryption of stored session data.

C.finding: Telemetry, error reports and recordings are protected; audit arguments and model-bound outputs are not.
C.gap: Model-bound messages and audit records are not redacted.

D.finding: Telemetry is enabled by default, content-free.

B.finding: Session cookies for every signed-in site are reachable by the model through raw CDP.
B.gap: Long-lived, high-privilege session credentials are reachable by the model.

criteria.name: Audit & traceability
criteria.question: Can you reconstruct what the agent did, for whom, and who approved it, from a record the agent couldn't alter?
criteria.summary: Every tool dispatch, including each browser primitive inside a `run` script as a child record, is written to a local SQLite audit log with session, agent label and arguments, plus screenshots and replayable recordings. The agent's identity is whatever name the client declares. Records are written after the action through an asynchronous worker and failures are only logged; guard rejections are not recorded. The log lives in ~/.browserclaw, is pruned after 7 days by default, and its retention and cleanup are driven through the local cockpit API.

S.finding: Structured per-call records with arguments, timing, and parent-child links for script primitives.
S.gap: Actor attribution relies on a self-declared agent name and the store has no tamper evidence.

criteria.name: Limits & kill switch
criteria.question: Are there hard limits on steps, time, and cost, and does stopping the agent actually stop everything?
criteria.summary: Each `run` and `evaluate` call is capped at 30 seconds, a cap the model cannot raise, and QuickJS scripts also have memory and stack limits and an interrupt that fires on cancellation or deadline. The cockpit can cancel a session, which cancels in-flight dispatches. There is no cap on the number of calls, sessions or open tabs, and no rate limit on actions. Page-side work started by a script continues after a timeout or cancellation.

S.finding: Server-enforced timeouts and output caps on the script and evaluate tools, with an engine interrupt.
S.gap: No concurrency or rate limits on dispatch.

evidence.note: all hits are the max_concurrent_used_sessions analytics metric, test semaphores, or audit-worker internals; none limits tool dispatch concurrency or rate

C.finding: Per-call timeouts apply to tool work; sessions and tabs are not bounded.
C.gap: No bound across a session's calls or spawned tabs.

D.finding: Caps are clamped constants the model cannot raise.
D.gap: Hard ceilings exist but cover only per-call time.

B.finding: Cancellation ends in-flight dispatches, but page-side work and the agent's own loop continue unbounded.
B.gap: No session-level time or action ceiling.

critical_findings.summary: Agents act with every signed-in session in the browser profile, which default onboarding fills from Chrome; there is no per-request authorization.
Model-written scripts run in a C JavaScript engine inside the server process, which runs as the user and drives the signed-in browser.
A hijacked agent can leak private data and act irreversibly in signed-in accounts with no human involved.

evidence.contains: files must exist on the server filesystem

rule_of_two.untrusted_input: Arbitrary web pages read via read/snapshot/run (crates/browseros-mcp/src/tools/run.rs:36)
rule_of_two.sensitive_data: Imported logins and every signed-in session (apps/claw-onboard/src/onboarding/onboarding-v2.helpers.ts:109-113)
rule_of_two.state_change_or_egress: Clicks, navigation, uploads and raw CDP on any site (crates/browseros-mcp/src/tools/run.rs:71)

fixes.summary: Lock down the local cockpit API's default access configuration.
Require a human confirmation in the cockpit before save_skill links a skill into other agents and before helpers are persisted.
Wrap run script results in the same untrusted-content markers as the granular read tools.
Add accurate read/destructive annotations to act, navigate, download, upload and save_skill, and offer a server-enforced read-only mode.
Remove raw CDP from the default run SDK or restrict it to an allowlist of read-only methods.

reaudit_log.reason: QuickJS is a capability-only runtime but its engine is written in C; the L3 anchor requires a memory-safe runtime.
The injected raw CDP method is model-reachable, not an operator escape hatch, so the L3 coverage anchor is not met.
neo uses its own browser profile rather than the everyday Chrome profile, a dedicated but broadly scoped identity.

limitations: Static source review of the pinned commit only; nothing was executed, installed, or probed.

Scored BrowserOS neo (apps/claw-server-rust, crates/browseros-mcp, apps/claw-app and the neo Chromium build), which the README leads with. The classic BrowserOS AI browser in the same repo (apps/app and apps/server, with a built-in agent) was not scored.
neo is a tool server: approval, model choice and loop limits belong to the connected agent and are not credited here.
The Chromium patch set was reviewed only for the server launch, ports, proxy and remote-access defaults; the rest of the browser fork was not examined.
